conversation.content:
Hi there, Mom—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into your new role and to check in on how you’re feeling as you adjust to life with your baby. To do that, I’ll be using a quick screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the **EPDS**. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that ask about mood, anxiety, and how you’ve been coping over the past seven days. This isn’t a pass-or-fail quiz; it’s just one way we can make sure you’re getting the right support.

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me something that suggests you or someone else might be in danger—then we’d talk together about the safest next steps. Feel free to answer in your own words; there are no right or wrong answers, and we’ll take it at your pace.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly, not very often. I used to laugh all the time—my husband and I would joke around while we cooked dinner—but now it’s like I can’t quite get there. Maybe once or twice this week I cracked a smile at something silly the baby did, but it faded fast. Most of the time I’m too tired or just… flat, I guess.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really. I mean, I can see when something is supposed to be funny, but it just feels distant—like I’m watching it through a fog. I don’t remember the last time I actually laughed out loud.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much anymore. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more thing I have to get through. I still try to plan one small thing each day, but when it comes around I’m too tired or worried to really enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. When he wouldn’t nap yesterday I sat there crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom. Deep down I know babies just cry, but the guilt still hits every time.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure he’s going to choke, even though he’s fine. Or I’ll lie down and picture the crib collapsing or the stroller rolling into the street. I know it’s unlikely, but I can’t turn the thoughts off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s changed. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and watching the baby monitor like a hawk.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days. There’s always a bottle to wash, laundry piling up, and the baby wants to be held constantly. I’ll start one chore, hear him cry, drop everything, and by evening nothing’s finished and I feel like I’m drowning. I keep telling myself other moms manage, so why can’t I.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. Even when the baby finally settles, my mind keeps spinning—playing the day over, worrying about what I did wrong, imagining worst-case scenarios. It takes me an hour or more to fall asleep, and I wake up at 2 or 3 a.m. with my heart pounding, then lie there listening to every tiny noise from the crib.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s how most days feel. I wake up with this heavy, gray mood that just sticks around. I’ll look at the baby and feel love, but it’s like there’s a thick pane of glass between us—I can see the joy, but I can’t quite reach it.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried twice this week. Once when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was starving him, and again yesterday when my mom left after dropping off groceries. It just hit me how alone and useless I felt, even though she was trying to help.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It… it has crossed my mind. Just brief flashes—like wondering if everyone would be better off without me, or imagining not waking up. I’ve never planned anything, and I don’t want to die; I just want the scared, heavy feeling to stop.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has been replaced by a heavy, gray mood that shadows most days, along with constant worry, panicky surges, and exhausting guilt. It's clear you're working incredibly hard to care for your baby while feeling emotionally drained, overwhelmed, and sometimes hopeless.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes anhedonia and emotional detachment, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a marked drop in anticipation and enjoyment, still trying but unable to connect with pleasure, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense self-blame ('a lot,' 'terrible mom') that is clearly disproportionate to the situation, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>The patient describes experiencing intrusive, racing worries "pretty much every day" with vivid catastrophic images, matching the "Yes, very often" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic episodes occurring multiple times in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep (hour+ to fall asleep, wakes at 2–3 a.m.), clearly stating this happens "most of the time" and directly answering "Yes" to the question.</sym>, <sym>The response clearly describes persistent, pervasive sadness that dominates most days, directly matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying twice this week due to distressing situations, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 well exceeds the 14-point threshold for probable <med>postpartum depression</med> and indicates severe symptom load. You endorse daily <sym>low mood</sym>, loss of interest, disproportionate self-blame, <sym>anxiety</sym> with <sym>panic symptoms</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>fleeting suicidal thoughts</sym>. This pattern meets screening criteria for a Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and possible comorbid <med>panic disorder</med>. Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Request a full safety evaluation including self-harm risk and supports plan
3. Ask about starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med>, an <med>SSRI</med>, or both
4. Share these results with a trusted family member so they can help schedule care and stay with you if needed
5. Plan brief respite: accept help with night feeds, use 20-min rest windows, and practice 4-7-8 breathing when panicky
6. Call 988 or local emergency services immediately if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant age not specified  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [Clinician name, credentials]

Presenting Concerns  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Intrusive, unrealistic anxiety (infant safety) with panic-like episodes  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia secondary to rumination  
- Feeling “drowning”/overwhelmed; chores frequently unfinished  
- Brief passive self-harm ideation without active plan or intent (Q10)

Key Symptoms Endorsed (EPDS equivalents)  
Q1–Q2: Loss of pleasure/enjoyment (score 3 each)  
Q3: Excessive guilt (score 3)  
Q4–Q5: Chronic anxiety + panic attacks (score 3 each)  
Q6: Perceives coping failure (score 3)  
Q7–Q9: Sleep disruption, persistent sadness, crying (score 3 each)  
Q10: Passive suicidal thoughts (score 3)

Pattern  
Consistent with elevated risk for Major Depressive Episode with anxious features and possible comorbid Panic Disorder, all postpartum onset.

Risk Flags  
- Passive suicidal ideation present → Safety assessment required  
- Daily panic symptoms impairing functioning  
- Insomnia compounding mood liability  
- Strong maternal guilt/cognitive distortions

Screening Impression  
High screening probability for moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; immediate safety evaluation and follow-up with OB/GYN or perinatal mental health specialist recommended. Consider formal EPDS scoring and development of safety plan before end of visit.
